source_batch.unit_label: Module A: International Banking - External Commercial Borrowings and Foreign Investments in India

facts.statement: Foreign direct investment (FDI) means investment through equity instruments by a person resident outside India in an unlisted Indian company, or in ten per cent or more of the post-issue paid-up equity capital on a fully diluted basis of a listed Indian company. If an existing investment in a listed company falls below ten per cent it continues to be treated as FDI. Fully diluted basis means the total number of shares that would be outstanding if all possible sources of conversion were exercised. Foreign investment means any investment by a person resident outside India on a repatriable basis in equity instruments of an Indian company or in the capital of an LLP; a person resident outside India may hold foreign investment either as FDI or as foreign portfolio investment (FPI) in a particular company. Foreign portfolio investment means investment through equity instruments of less than ten per cent of the post-issue paid-up share capital on a fully diluted basis of a listed Indian company (or less than ten per cent of the paid-up value of each series of equity instrument). An FPI (the investor) is a person registered under the SEBI FPI Regulations, 2014.

Equity instruments are equity shares, convertible debentures, preference shares and share warrants issued by an Indian company. Equity shares include partly paid shares; convertible debentures and preference shares mean fully and mandatorily convertible instruments that are fully paid; partly paid shares issued to a non-resident must be fully called up within twelve months and twenty-five per cent of the total consideration, including premium, must be received upfront; for share warrants at least twenty-five per cent must be received upfront and the balance within eighteen months; equity instruments can carry an optionality clause subject to a minimum lock-in of one year (or as prescribed for the sector, whichever is higher) but without any option or right to exit at an assured price.

Sectors prohibited for FDI: lottery business including government or private and online lotteries; gambling and betting including casinos; chit funds; Nidhi companies; trading in transferable development rights; real estate business or construction of farm houses (real estate business being dealing in land and immovable property to earn profit, excluding townships, residential or commercial premises, roads, bridges, educational institutions, recreational facilities, city and regional infrastructure, broking and REITs and rental income); manufacturing of cigars, cheroots, cigarillos and cigarettes of tobacco or tobacco substitutes; and activities not open to private sector investment such as atomic energy and railway operations (except permitted activities).

Downstream investment is investment by an Indian entity that has received indirect foreign investment; such an entity must comply with the entry route, sectoral caps, pricing guidelines and conditions applicable to foreign investment. Downstream investment that counts as indirect foreign investment needs Board approval and any shareholders' agreement; the investing entity must bring in funds from abroad and not use funds borrowed in the domestic market, though internal accruals (profits transferred to reserves after tax) may be used. Any equity holding by a non-resident resulting from conversion of debt is reckoned for total foreign investment; FCCBs and DRs with debt underlying are not.

Pledge of shares: a promoter of a borrowing company that has raised an ECB may pledge the shares of the borrowing company or its resident associates to secure the ECB, co-terminous with the ECB, with the statutory auditor's certificate on end-use and an authorised dealer's no-objection; a non-resident holding equity instruments may pledge them in favour of a bank in India for credit facilities to the Indian company for bona fide purposes, in favour of an overseas bank for credit to such person or the company's promoter or overseas group company, or in favour of a registered NBFC for bona fide credit to the Indian company, subject to the authorised dealer satisfying itself of compliance; on invocation, transfer follows the entry route, sectoral caps, pricing and conditions at the time of creating the pledge.

Schedule III (investment by an individual person resident outside India, including an NRI or OCI, on a repatriation basis, in a listed Indian company on a recognised stock exchange): purchases and sales through a branch designated by an authorised dealer; holding of any one individual must be less than ten per cent of paid-up equity capital on a fully diluted basis (or of each series of debentures, preference shares or warrants); holdings of all such individuals together must not exceed twenty-four per cent; holdings under Schedules II, III and any other schedule are aggregated against the ten per cent limit. A breach of the individual limit must be divested within five trading days of the settlement date of the trades causing it, failing which the entire investment is treated as FDI and no further portfolio investment may be made in that company; the designated branch brings the breach to the notice of depositories and the company within seven trading days of settlement. In addition an NRI or OCI may without limit buy or sell units of domestic mutual funds investing more than 50 per cent in equity, and shares in public sector enterprises being disinvested by the Government, and may subscribe to the National Pension System. The widening from NRIs and OCIs to all individuals resident outside India took effect on 12 June 2026 and was operationalised by RBI on 15 June 2026.
facts.locator: Schedule III; RBI A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 14 of 15 June 2026

facts.statement: Schedule IV (NRI or OCI, including a company, trust or partnership firm abroad owned and controlled by NRIs or OCIs, on a non-repatriation basis): they may purchase equity instruments of an Indian company, units of an investment vehicle and the capital of an LLP without limit, on or off the stock exchange, and convertible notes of startups; the investment is deemed domestic investment at par with residents; units of domestic mutual funds that invest more than 50 per cent in equity may be bought or sold without limit; they may not invest under this Schedule in a Nidhi company or a company engaged in agricultural or plantation activities, real estate business, construction of farm houses or dealing in transferable development rights. An NRI or OCI may invest on a non-repatriation basis by contributing to the capital of a firm or proprietary concern in India provided it is not engaged in agricultural or plantation activity, print media or real estate business.
facts.locator: Schedule IV, parts A and B

facts.statement: Authorised dealers may allow NRIs and PIOs, on documentary evidence, to remit up to USD one million per financial year, including transfers to NRE and SNRR accounts, out of NRO balances, sale proceeds of assets and assets acquired by inheritance or legacy; where the remittance is from an NRO account the dealer obtains an undertaking that it is made from the remitter's legitimate receivables in India, not borrowed from any person nor transferred from another NRO account, failing which the holder is liable to penal action under FEMA. For residential property the repatriation of sale proceeds is restricted to not more than two properties. All instalments are remitted through the same authorised dealer.
facts.locator: Paragraph 3.2; RBI FAQ on purchase of immovable property, Part II Q7

facts.statement: The courseware (S03 printed pp. 79-82 and 170-176) states the same concepts: FDI and FPI by the ten per cent test, eligible instruments, closed sectors, pledge rules, the Portfolio Investment Scheme limits of 5 and 10 per cent (superseded on 12 June 2026), a ten-year lock-in on remitting proceeds of property acquired while resident (not found in the current Remittance of Assets Master Direction), and investment without limit on a non-repatriation basis in specified government securities, treasury bills, money market funds and National Savings Certificates.

payload.title: FDI, FPI and foreign investment: the ten per cent line
payload.core_explanation_md:
Everything in foreign investment starts from **one test: how much of a company does the non-resident hold, and is it listed?**

- **FDI**: investment in **equity instruments** by a person resident outside India in
  - an **unlisted** Indian company (any amount), or
  - **10% or more** of the **post-issue paid-up equity capital, on a fully diluted basis**, of a **listed** company.
- **FPI (portfolio investment)**: **less than 10%** of a **listed** company's equity on a fully diluted basis.
- **Once FDI, always FDI**: if a holding in a listed company **falls below 10%**, it **still counts as FDI**.
- **Fully diluted** means all shares that would be outstanding **if every conversion right were exercised**.
- **Foreign investment** is the umbrella: investment on a **repatriable basis** in equity instruments of an Indian company or the capital of an **LLP**. One investor may hold **either FDI or FPI in a given company**.
- An **FPI** (the investor) is a person **registered with SEBI** under the FPI Regulations, 2014.

payload.title: What counts as an equity instrument, and the 25% rule on part-paid shares and warrants
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Equity instruments** = **equity shares**, **convertible debentures**, **preference shares** and **share warrants** issued by an Indian company.

- **Equity shares** include **partly paid** shares.
- **Convertible debentures** and **preference shares** count only if **fully and mandatorily convertible** and **fully paid**.
- **Partly paid shares** issued to a non-resident: **25% of the total consideration (premium included) upfront** and the shares **fully called up within 12 months**.
- **Share warrants**: **at least 25% upfront**, the **balance within 18 months**.
- An **optionality clause** is allowed only with a **minimum lock-in of one year** (or the sector's period, whichever is higher) and **no assured-price exit**.

payload.title: Sectors closed to foreign direct investment
payload.core_explanation_md:
**No FDI** in:

1. **Lottery** business (government, private, online).
2. **Gambling and betting**, including **casinos**.
3. **Chit funds**.
4. **Nidhi companies**.
5. **Trading in transferable development rights (TDR)**.
6. **Real estate business** or **construction of farm houses**. (Real estate business means dealing in land and property **to earn profit**; it **excludes** townships, residential or commercial premises, roads, bridges, educational and recreational facilities, city-level infrastructure, **broking**, **REITs** and **rental income**.)
7. **Manufacture of cigars, cheroots, cigarillos and cigarettes** of tobacco or tobacco substitutes.
8. Activities **not open to private investment**, such as **atomic energy** and **railway operations** (except permitted activities).

payload.title: Downstream investment: foreign money passed on through an Indian company
payload.core_explanation_md:
When an **Indian entity that has received indirect foreign investment** (one that is **owned or controlled by non-residents**) invests in **another Indian company**, the investee is treated as having **indirect foreign investment**, and must meet the **entry route, sectoral cap, pricing guidelines and conditions** that apply to foreign investment.

**Conditions on the investing entity**
- **Board approval** (and any shareholders' agreement).
- **Bring funds from abroad**; do **not** use funds **borrowed in the domestic market**. **Internal accruals** (profits moved to reserves **after tax**) are fine.

**Counting rules**
- Shares a non-resident gets by **converting debt** are **counted** as foreign investment.
- **FCCBs and DRs with debt underlying** are **not** counted.

payload.title: Pledging shares: who may pledge, to whom, and what happens on invocation
Individuals abroad buying listed shares: the 10% and 24% limits
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Who**: since **12 June 2026**, **any individual resident outside India**, not only NRIs and OCIs (RBI operationalised it on **15 June 2026**).

**How**: buy and sell on a **recognised stock exchange**, through a **branch designated by an authorised dealer**.

**Limits**
- **One individual**: **less than 10%** of the company's paid-up equity on a fully diluted basis. Holdings under **Schedules II, III and any other schedule** are **added** for this test.
- **All such individuals together**: **not more than 24%**.

**If the 10% limit is breached**: **divest within five trading days** of the settlement date of the trades that caused it. The designated branch tells the **depositories and the company within seven trading days**. If the person does **not** divest, the **whole investment becomes FDI** and **no further portfolio investment** is allowed in that company.

**NRIs and OCIs may also, without limit**: buy or sell **domestic mutual fund units** investing **more than 50% in equity**, buy **shares of public sector enterprises being disinvested by the Government**, and subscribe to the **National Pension System**.

payload.title: NRIs investing on a non-repatriation basis: what is open and what is closed
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Open, without any limit** (on or off the exchange): **equity instruments** of Indian companies, **units of investment vehicles**, **capital of an LLP**, **convertible notes of startups**, and **mutual fund units** investing **more than 50% in equity**. Such investment is treated as **domestic investment**, at par with residents.

**Closed**: no investment under this route in a **Nidhi company**, or a company in **agriculture or plantation**, **real estate business**, **farm house construction** or **TDRs**.

**Firms and proprietary concerns**: an NRI or OCI may put capital into a firm or proprietary concern on a non-repatriation basis if it is **not** in **agriculture or plantation**, **print media** or **real estate business**.

payload.title: Sending sale proceeds and NRO balances abroad: USD 1 million, undertakings and the property cap
payload.core_explanation_md:
**NRIs and PIOs** may remit up to **USD 1 million per financial year** (including transfers to **NRE** and **SNRR** accounts) out of **NRO balances**, **sale proceeds of assets** and **assets inherited**, on documentary evidence, through **one authorised dealer** if paid in instalments.

**NRO undertaking**: the bank takes a declaration that the money is the holder's **legitimate receivable in India**, **not borrowed** and **not transferred from another NRO account**, or the holder faces **action under FEMA**.

**Residential property**: repatriation of sale proceeds is limited to **not more than two properties**.

Older books speak of a **ten-year lock-in** for property acquired while resident. The current **Remittance of Assets** Master Direction (updated 29 June 2026) **does not contain it**.

payload.title: How many more shares may an individual abroad buy?
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a listed Indian company has 5,00,00,000 shares on a fully diluted basis. Individual B resident outside India already holds 9.4% of it. All individuals resident outside India together hold 1,05,00,000 shares under Schedule III. How many more shares can B buy?

worked_steps.description: The individual limit is LESS than 10%, so B must stay below 50,00,000 shares: at most one share short of the limit.
B is held to the smaller of the two headrooms.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: B can buy at most 2,99,999 more shares: the individual limit (less than 10%) binds before the 24% aggregate limit does

self_check.prompt_text: If B bought 3,00,000 more shares, what would the holding be, and what must happen?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Exactly 50,00,000 shares, which is 10%: not less than 10%, so the limit is breached and B must divest within five trading days of settlement, or the whole holding becomes FDI.

payload.title: The breach clock: five and seven trading days
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: trades that take an individual abroad over the 10% limit settle on Tuesday 7 July 2026. Count trading days as Monday to Friday with no exchange holidays. By when must the holding be divested, and by when must the designated branch tell the depositories and the company?

worked_steps.description: Five trading days after settlement: Wed 8, Thu 9, Fri 10, Mon 13, Tue 14 July.
Seven trading days after settlement: add Wed 15 and Thu 16 July.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Divest by Tuesday 14 July 2026; the designated branch reports by Thursday 16 July 2026

self_check.prompt_text: If the individual does not divest by 14 July, what happens to the earlier part of the holding?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The entire investment in that company is treated as FDI, and no further portfolio investment can be made in it.

- **Equity shares** include **partly paid** shares.

- **Partly paid shares** issued to a non-resident: **25% of the total consideration (premium included) upfront** and the shares **fully called up within 12 months**.
- **Share warrants**: **at least 25% upfront**, the **balance within 18 months**.
- An **optionality clause** is allowed only with a **minimum lock-in of one year** (or the sector's period, whichever is higher) and **no assured-price exit**.

items.title: Sectors closed to foreign direct investment
items.core_explanation_md:
**No FDI** in:

1. **Lottery** business (government, private, online).
2. **Gambling and betting**, including **casinos**.
3. **Chit funds**.
4. **Nidhi companies**.
5. **Trading in transferable development rights (TDR)**.
6. **Real estate business** or **construction of farm houses**. (Real estate business means dealing in land and property **to earn profit**; it **excludes** townships, residential or commercial premises, roads, bridges, educational and recreational facilities, city-level infrastructure, **broking**, **REITs** and **rental income**.)
7. **Manufacture of cigars, cheroots, cigarillos and cigarettes** of tobacco or tobacco substitutes.
8. Activities **not open to private investment**, such as **atomic energy** and **railway operations** (except permitted activities).

items.title: Downstream investment: foreign money passed on through an Indian company
items.core_explanation_md:
When an **Indian entity that has received indirect foreign investment** (one that is **owned or controlled by non-residents**) invests in **another Indian company**, the investee is treated as having **indirect foreign investment**, and must meet the **entry route, sectoral cap, pricing guidelines and conditions** that apply to foreign investment.

**Conditions on the investing entity**
- **Board approval** (and any shareholders' agreement).
- **Bring funds from abroad**; do **not** use funds **borrowed in the domestic market**. **Internal accruals** (profits moved to reserves **after tax**) are fine.

**Counting rules**
- Shares a non-resident gets by **converting debt** are **counted** as foreign investment.
- **FCCBs and DRs with debt underlying** are **not** counted.

items.title: Individuals abroad buying listed shares: the 10% and 24% limits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who**: since **12 June 2026**, **any individual resident outside India**, not only NRIs and OCIs (RBI operationalised it on **15 June 2026**).

**How**: buy and sell on a **recognised stock exchange**, through a **branch designated by an authorised dealer**.

**Limits**
- **One individual**: **less than 10%** of the company's paid-up equity on a fully diluted basis. Holdings under **Schedules II, III and any other schedule** are **added** for this test.
- **All such individuals together**: **not more than 24%**.

**If the 10% limit is breached**: **divest within five trading days** of the settlement date of the trades that caused it. The designated branch tells the **depositories and the company within seven trading days**. If the person does **not** divest, the **whole investment becomes FDI** and **no further portfolio investment** is allowed in that company.

**NRIs and OCIs may also, without limit**: buy or sell **domestic mutual fund units** investing **more than 50% in equity**, buy **shares of public sector enterprises being disinvested by the Government**, and subscribe to the **National Pension System**.

items.title: NRIs investing on a non-repatriation basis: what is open and what is closed
items.core_explanation_md:
**Open, without any limit** (on or off the exchange): **equity instruments** of Indian companies, **units of investment vehicles**, **capital of an LLP**, **convertible notes of startups**, and **mutual fund units** investing **more than 50% in equity**. Such investment is treated as **domestic investment**, at par with residents.

**Closed**: no investment under this route in a **Nidhi company**, or a company in **agriculture or plantation**, **real estate business**, **farm house construction** or **TDRs**.

**Firms and proprietary concerns**: an NRI or OCI may put capital into a firm or proprietary concern on a non-repatriation basis if it is **not** in **agriculture or plantation**, **print media** or **real estate business**.

items.title: Sending sale proceeds and NRO balances abroad: USD 1 million, undertakings and the property cap
items.core_explanation_md:
**NRIs and PIOs** may remit up to **USD 1 million per financial year** (including transfers to **NRE** and **SNRR** accounts) out of **NRO balances**, **sale proceeds of assets** and **assets inherited**, on documentary evidence, through **one authorised dealer** if paid in instalments.

**NRO undertaking**: the bank takes a declaration that the money is the holder's **legitimate receivable in India**, **not borrowed** and **not transferred from another NRO account**, or the holder faces **action under FEMA**.

**Residential property**: repatriation of sale proceeds is limited to **not more than two properties**.

Older books speak of a **ten-year lock-in** for property acquired while resident. The current **Remittance of Assets** Master Direction (updated 29 June 2026) **does not contain it**.

items.title: How many more shares may an individual abroad buy?
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a listed Indian company has 5,00,00,000 shares on a fully diluted basis. Individual B resident outside India already holds 9.4% of it. All individuals resident outside India together hold 1,05,00,000 shares under Schedule III. How many more shares can B buy?

worked_steps.description: The individual limit is LESS than 10%, so B must stay below 50,00,000 shares: at most one share short of the limit.
B is held to the smaller of the two headrooms.

items.final_answer_with_unit: B can buy at most 2,99,999 more shares: the individual limit (less than 10%) binds before the 24% aggregate limit does

self_check.expected_takeaway: Exactly 50,00,000 shares, which is 10%: not less than 10%, so the limit is breached and B must divest within five trading days of settlement, or the whole holding becomes FDI.

items.title: The breach clock: five and seven trading days
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: trades that take an individual abroad over the 10% limit settle on Tuesday 7 July 2026. Count trading days as Monday to Friday with no exchange holidays. worked_steps.description: Five trading days after settlement: Wed 8, Thu 9, Fri 10, Mon 13, Tue 14 July.
Seven trading days after settlement: add Wed 15 and Thu 16 July.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Divest by Tuesday 14 July 2026; the designated branch reports by Thursday 16 July 2026
